newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian space launch marred by failed docking.
newsitem.headline: Russian space launch marred by failed docking.

text.p: Russia launched the first satellite from a new cosmodrome on Tuesday, but celebrations were marred by a row over its threat to the environment and a problem with the Mir orbiting station.
A secret military satellite went into orbit at 0200 GMT aboard a modified SS-25 ballistic missile, now called the Start-1 booster rocket .

It blasted off from the Svobodny cosmodrome in the Far East which is still under construction at a snowbound former strategic nuclear missile base in Siberia about 9,000 km (6,000 miles) east of Moscow.

The new cosmodrome, only 100 km (60 miles) from the Chinese border, was developed on orders from President Boris Yeltsin to to reduce dependence on the main Soviet launch site at Baikonur, which Moscow now has to rent from independent Kazakhstan.
Baikonur's maintenance and rent -- $115 million a year -- are the source of endless squabbles between Moscow and Almaty.
"Russia cannot be dependent on Baikonur forever and pay rent to Kazakhstan," said Pyotr Lebedev, deputy commander of Svobodny, which means "Free" in Russian.

The base should eventually become Russia's main launch site due to its good position on the same latitude as Baikonur, although there are no immediate plans to transfer launches of manned space flights from Baikonur.
But the successful launch prompted a dispute with the authorities of the ethnic region of Yakutia.

Under a 1996 agreement between Moscow and Yakutia, the ethnic northern republic allowed Russia to jettison parts of spent booster rockets over its thinly populated territory, but Tuesday's launch was not fully approved by Yakutia officials.

Yegor Borisov, deputy head of the diamond-rich ethnic republic's government, told Interfax news agency he was filing a suit against the head of Russia's military space forces because the launch had not been authorised by Yakutia.
Interfax said the authorities would also recommend that the local parliament scrap the treaty between Moscow and Yakutia.

Russia's financially troubled space programme also suffered a new setback on Tuesday, when an unmanned Russian Progress-M-33 cargo spacecraft failed to dock with the manned orbiting module of the ageing space station Mir.

The Progress, in orbit since November 1996, had undocked from Mir on February 6 to make way for a Soyuz TM-25 craft which brought a replacement crew. Itar-Tass news agency said two redocking attempts had now failed.
It quoted a mission control spokesman as saying experts were looking into the reasons for the failures and were deciding whether to make another docking attempt.

It was the second hitch in just over a week to trouble the 11-year-old Mir, which has already outlived its expected lifespan. On February 23, a fire broke out on board, forcing the crew to don gas masks.

Russia's space agency is suffering a severe cash crisis which last week prompted it to postpone the launch of its first contribution to a planned international space station, Alpha, which will replace Mir.
The new Svobodny cosmodrome is destined to be the main launch pad for the commercial satellites, on which Moscow is pinning big hopes.
